days.title: The strongest material on Earth
days.hook: Graphene is about 200 times stronger than steel — yet it's almost transparent.
days.caption:
One atom thick. Nearly see-through (it absorbs only ~2.3% of light). And, weight for weight, around 200× stronger than steel.

Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb lattice — and it could reshape batteries, electronics and aerospace.

#science #graphene #materials #engineering

Roughly two-thirds of an octopus's ~500 million neurons sit in its arms. Each arm can taste, touch and make decisions semi-independently.

Eight arms. One brain. A distributed mind.

days.caption:
A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a ball about 20 km across.

The result: a teaspoon of its matter would weigh around a billion tons on Earth — roughly the weight of every human alive, many times over.

days.title: Your brain runs on tiny electrical storms

days.caption:
86 billion neurons, firing tiny electrical signals every second — and the whole system runs on roughly 20 watts.

That's about the power of a dim light bulb, and far more efficient than any supercomputer.

(Note: the brain uses this energy; it can't power a bulb itself.)

It smashes particles together at nearly the speed of light — and in 2012 it helped confirm the Higgs boson.

#LHC #CERN #physics #engineering

days.caption:
Tardigrades (water bears) are about half a millimetre long. Dry them out and they curl into a 'tun' state that can survive extreme cold, intense radiation — even exposure to open space.

days.title: Why sunsets are red
days.hook: Sunsets turn red because blue light gets scattered away more easily than red light.
stat: more scattering for blue than red
days.caption:
Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths far more than long (red) ones — that's Rayleigh scattering.

At sunset, light crosses much more atmosphere, so the blue is scattered away before it reaches you. What's left: orange and red.

#sunset #physics #science #nature

scenes.vo: At sunset, light travels through much more air. The blue gets scattered away. Only the reds and oranges make it to your eyes.

days.payoff: Every sunset is physics, painted across the sky.

That's fast enough to fly from New York to Tokyo in under a minute.

days.title: Why bridges don't just fall
days.hook: Suspension bridges carry massive loads by turning weight into tension in the cables and compression in the towers.

days.caption:
The deck hangs from vertical suspenders. Those pull on the main cables (tension). The cables pass over the towers, pushing them down into the ground (compression), and are anchored into huge blocks at each end.

Weight isn't resisted — it's redirected.

#engineering #bridges #architecture #physics

days.caption:
The earliest shark-like fish date back roughly 450 million years. The first true trees appeared around 385 million years ago.

Sharks have outlived dinosaurs and survived five mass extinctions.

days.caption:
Earth's molten iron core generates a magnetic field — the magnetosphere — that deflects most of the charged particles streaming from the Sun.

The auroras are where some of those particles leak in near the poles.

The 500 Series got a kingfisher-shaped nose: quieter, about 10% faster, and roughly 15% less electricity used.

days.title: Why airplanes survive lightning
days.hook: On average, every commercial airliner is struck by lightning about once a year — and it's built to handle it.
stat: lightning strikes per airliner, on average
days.caption:
Lightning usually hits a nose or wingtip, travels along the conductive outer skin, and exits from another extremity like the tail. The cabin acts like a Faraday cage.

Composite planes have embedded metal mesh to do the same job.

days.title: The smell of rain

days.caption:
That earthy smell after rain is petrichor. Raindrops hitting dry soil launch tiny aerosols carrying plant oils and geosmin, a compound made by soil bacteria.

days.title: Black holes don't suck

It would get very dark and cold — but we wouldn't fall in.

days.title: Why cats land on their feet
days.hook: Cats twist in midair using a 'righting reflex' — and it doesn't break any laws of physics.
days.caption:
A falling cat bends at the middle and rotates its front and back halves in opposite directions, tucking and extending its legs to control each half's spin.

Net angular momentum stays zero — physics stays happy, and the cat lands upright.

days.title: Why volcanoes make fertile land
days.hook: Some of the most fertile soil on Earth exists because volcanoes break down into nutrient-rich minerals.
days.caption:
Volcanic ash and rock weather into soils rich in minerals like potassium, phosphorus and magnesium. That's why the slopes of volcanoes from Java to Italy are covered in farms and vineyards.

Destruction, given time, becomes life.

days.title: The physics of a boomerang
days.hook: A boomerang comes back because of lift, spin, and a clever imbalance in airflow.
days.caption:
Each arm of a boomerang is a small wing. As it spins, the arm moving forward meets faster air and makes more lift than the other one.

That uneven push tilts the spinning boomerang (gyroscopic precession), steering it around in a circle — back to you.

#physics #boomerang #science #explainer

days.title: Why astronauts grow in space
days.hook: Astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller in space because the spine expands in microgravity.
days.caption:
Without gravity compressing them, the discs between the vertebrae expand. Astronauts can gain up to ~3% in height — around 5 cm.

It disappears within months back on Earth, and often brings back pain with it.

#space #astronaut #humanbody #NASA

days.title: The strongest bite in the animal kingdom
days.hook: Saltwater crocodiles have the most powerful bite ever measured — about 3,700 psi.
days.caption:
In 2012, researchers measured a saltwater crocodile bite of about 3,700 psi (16,460 newtons) — the strongest ever recorded in a living animal.

For comparison, a human bite is around 160 psi.

#crocodile #animals #nature #science

days.title: How skyscrapers survive wind
days.hook: Tall buildings are designed to sway — because resisting wind completely would be more dangerous.
days.caption:
Rigid structures crack; flexible ones survive. Many skyscrapers sway a little on purpose, and some use a tuned mass damper — Taipei 101 hangs a 660-tonne steel sphere near its top that swings against the motion.

#architecture #engineering #skyscraper #physics

days.title: The coldest place in the universe is on Earth
days.hook: Scientists have created temperatures far colder than deep space — inside laboratories on Earth.
stat: deep space — labs reach billionths of a kelvin
days.caption:
Deep space sits at about 2.7 K (−270.4 °C), warmed by the afterglow of the Big Bang. Using lasers and magnetic traps, labs have cooled atoms to billionths of a degree above absolute zero.

The coldest known places in the universe might be human-made.

#physics #quantum #science #absolutezero

days.title: Why flamingos are pink
days.hook: Flamingos are pink because of pigments in the food they eat.
days.caption:
Flamingo chicks hatch grey-white. Their pink comes from carotenoid pigments in algae and brine shrimp they eat — the same family of pigments that makes carrots orange.

Diet changes, colour fades.

Light takes time to travel. When the James Webb Space Telescope captures a galaxy 13 billion light-years away, we see it as it was 13 billion years ago.

Every deep-field image is a time machine.

days.title: Why helicopters can hover
days.hook: A helicopter hovers by balancing lift, weight, torque and control — all at the same time.
days.caption:
Main rotor blades are spinning wings that create lift. Spinning them twists the body the other way (torque), so the tail rotor pushes back. Tilting the rotor disc steers the whole aircraft.

Hovering is constant, precise balance.

#helicopter #aviation #physics #engineering

days.title: The future of robots
days.hook: Humanoid robots are getting better not because they look human — but because our world was designed for human bodies.
stat: legs and hands — the shape our world expects
days.caption:
Stairs, door handles, tools, car seats, kitchen counters — everything is shaped for two legs and two hands.

That's why companies are racing to build humanoid robots: the shape fits the world we already have.
